unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Exchange Rates and Forex Business

facts.statement: The Act defines "foreign currency" as any currency other than Indian currency, and "foreign exchange" as foreign currency including (i) deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency, (ii) drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in any foreign currency, and (iii) drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange drawn by banks, institutions or persons outside India but payable in Indian currency. "Currency" includes notes, postal notes, postal orders, money orders, cheques, drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit, bills of exchange, promissory notes, credit cards and similar instruments notified by the Reserve Bank.

A capital account transaction alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India, or assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India. A current account transaction is any other transaction and includes payments in connection with foreign trade, other current business, services and short-term banking and credit facilities in the ordinary course of business; payments of interest on loans and net income from investments; remittances for living expenses of parents, spouse and children abroad; and expenses of foreign travel, education and medical care of parents, spouse and children. An authorised person is an authorised dealer, money changer, off-shore banking unit or other person authorised by the Reserve Bank under section 10(1). A person resident in India is a person residing in India for more than 182 days in the preceding financial year (with exceptions for those who left or stay abroad for employment, business or an uncertain period), any person or body corporate registered or incorporated in India, and offices, branches or agencies in India owned or controlled by a non-resident or abroad owned or controlled by a resident.

Save as otherwise provided, no person shall deal in or transfer foreign exchange or foreign security to anyone who is not an authorised person; make any payment to or for the credit of a person resident outside India; receive, otherwise than through an authorised person, any payment by order or on behalf of a person resident outside India; or enter into a financial transaction in India as consideration for acquiring or creating, or transferring a right to acquire, an asset outside India (section 3). No person resident in India shall acquire, hold, own, possess or transfer foreign exchange, foreign security or immovable property outside India, save as the Act permits (section 4). Any person may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for a current account transaction, though the Central Government may impose reasonable restrictions in the public interest in consultation with the Reserve Bank (section 5). For capital account transactions the Reserve Bank and the Central Government may specify permissible classes, limits and conditions; a resident may hold foreign currency, security or immovable property abroad that he acquired or held when resident outside India or inherited from a non-resident (section 6).

The Reserve Bank may authorise persons as authorised dealers, money changers or off-shore banking units, and may revoke authorisation in public interest or for non-compliance after giving a reasonable opportunity to represent. An authorised person must follow the Reserve Bank's directions and must, before any transaction, require the customer's declaration and information that will reasonably satisfy it the transaction is not designed to contravene or evade the Act; if the customer refuses or complies unsatisfactorily, the authorised person must refuse in writing and report to the Reserve Bank if it believes contravention is contemplated (section 10). A person who buys foreign exchange for a declared purpose and does not use it for that purpose or surrender it within the specified period, or uses it for a non-permissible purpose, is deemed to have contravened the Act. The Reserve Bank may give authorised persons directions, require information, and penalise contravention of a direction or failure to file a return with a penalty up to Rs ten thousand and up to Rs two thousand a day for a continuing contravention (section 11), and may inspect authorised persons (section 12).

A person who contravenes the Act, or a rule, regulation, notification, direction or order under it, or a condition of an authorisation, is liable on adjudication to a penalty of up to three times the sum involved where the amount is quantifiable, or up to Rs two lakh where it is not, and for a continuing contravention a further penalty of up to Rs five thousand for every day after the first day (section 13(1)). A person who acquires foreign exchange, foreign security or immovable property abroad above the prescribed threshold is liable to a penalty of up to three times the sum involved and confiscation of equivalent value in India (section 13(1A)).

Under RBI's Internal Control Guidelines, the cardinal principle of operations in trading is clear functional segregation of dealing, mid-office, back-office (processing and control), accounting and reconciliation; for banks that trade actively the front office is the dealing room, the mid-office handles risk management, accounting policies and management information, and the back office handles settlement, reconciliation and accounting. Dealers should not be entrusted with accounting work; deals are recorded on deal slips (name of broker, counterparty, currencies, amounts, time, rate, due dates) that go without delay to the back office; the trading date, time and serial number are entered automatically by the system and cannot be altered by the dealer without authorisation; late deals are marked and passed to an official unconnected with the dealer. Voice recorders are desirable in dealing rooms, with tapes kept at least two months and, where a dispute arises, until it is resolved. Dealers take an annual compulsory continuous break of two weeks or longer, and acknowledge in writing and abide by the FEDAI and FIMMDA codes of conduct.

The back office must obtain independent confirmation of contracts (other than deals put through CCIL), dealers must never sign confirmations, discrepancies are rectified the same day and there is no backlog of confirmations; position and funds registers are kept updated; and where the system does not provide it, rate-scan reports are prepared at least three times a day and deals at wide variance from market rates are enquired into. Exchange brokers may not act as principals or maintain positions; broker's notes are received before the close of business on the day of the deal and reconciled the same day; nomination of brokers for deals not put through their medium is not permitted; ideally at least five or six brokers are empanelled and the panel reviewed annually; dealing staff have nothing to do with scrutiny and payment of brokerage claims; a monthly broker-wise payment statement goes to management; malpractices by brokers are reported to FEDAI; substitution of one bank by another in an inter-bank contract by a broker is prohibited.

Risk control systems must match the scale, complexity and risk content of the trading; senior management must closely oversee hedging products and prior approval is needed for any new product or change in design; policies are approved by the Board or a Board-authorised committee. The main risks are credit risk (pre-settlement risk, the replacement cost if a counterparty defaults during the life of the contract, and settlement risk, the risk of performing before the counterparty), liquidity risk, gap or interest rate risk, legal risk (managed by internationally accepted master agreements such as ISDA, IFEMA and ICOM) and operational risk (appropriate data processing and a written contingency plan). Global limits are set for local inter-bank business and overseas transactions; every dealer is advised of his limit; all deals are accounted against limits and positions aggregated at close of business to ensure the overnight limit, net open position and gap limits are not exceeded; excesses are reported to senior management and approved; breaches of regulatory limits are promptly reported to the Reserve Bank; value-at-risk models are reviewed periodically; reporting is done by officials not directly concerned with trading.

Documentation: for forward contracts of up to 13 months between banks and customers, a specific stamped contract note for each transaction; for inter-bank deals, unsigned computer-generated confirmations backed by a one-time stamped letter of indemnity; for forward contracts of more than 13 months and other derivatives between banks and with other customers, an ISDA Master Agreement with signed confirmations for each transaction; retail customers as in the first case; banks obtain a Board resolution from corporate clients authorising officials to deal. Records are preserved for the statutory retention period or as per internal guidelines.

Reconciliation of Nostro balances is an essential control: bank statements are received at least weekly and reconciled against the mirror account on the same date; unreconciled items are acted on continuously; transactions such as export bills purchased, drafts and travellers cheques issued and inward bills are put through suspense accounts to reduce unreconciled items; no set-off of debit or credit items or write-off of unreconciled items to profit and loss except as permitted; a monthly report from the reconciliation department shows progress, large and age-wise unreconciled items. Vostro accounts are monitored for funds flow, concealed overdrafts and credit risk (assessed at least once in twelve months), and balances are confirmed periodically. Dealing hours for USD/INR follow FEDAI; the bank's policy states whether off-premises and after-hours deals are allowed. Internal audit reviews limit excesses; a special audit of the dealing room and its systems is done at least once a year; concurrent audit is part of the early-warning system.

Authorised dealers' foreign exchange exposure limits are dual: a net overnight open position limit (NOOPL) for the capital charge on forex risk, which the Board fixes and communicates to the Reserve Bank and which must not exceed 25 per cent of total capital (Tier I and Tier II); and a limit for positions involving the rupee (NOP-INR) that the Reserve Bank may prescribe. For Indian banks the limits are aggregate for all branches including overseas branches and offshore banking units; for foreign banks only their Indian branches. The open position in a currency is the sum of the net spot, net forward and net options positions. The overall net open position uses the shorthand method: the net position in each currency and in gold is converted into rupees; the sum of all net short positions and the sum of all net long positions are found; the overall net foreign exchange position is the higher of the two. Offshore exposures are calculated standalone and not netted with onshore exposures. Aggregate gap limits (AGL) fixed by the Board must not exceed six times total capital, though dealers with tenor-wise PV01 and VaR limits may set their own. The ALCO or internal audit committee monitors adherence to the limits.

payload.title: What the Act means by foreign exchange, and by capital and current account
payload.core_explanation_md:
The statute gives precise definitions.

**Foreign currency** = **any currency other than Indian currency**.

**Foreign exchange** = foreign currency **and**:
1. **deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency**;
2. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency**;
3. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange drawn by banks, institutions or persons outside India but payable in Indian currency**.

**Capital account transaction**: one that **alters the assets or liabilities**, including contingent liabilities, **outside India of residents**, or **in India of non-residents**.

**Current account transaction**: **any other**, including payments for **foreign trade**, other current business and services, **short-term banking and credit facilities** in the ordinary course; **interest on loans and net investment income**; **remittances for living expenses** of parents, spouse and children abroad; and **foreign travel, education and medical care** of parents, spouse and children.

payload.title: Sections 3 to 6: the four basic rules of the Act
Sections 10 to 12: what an authorised person must do, and what RBI can do
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Authorisation (s.10)**: the Reserve Bank **authorises** authorised dealers, money changers and offshore banking units, and may **revoke** the authorisation in the **public interest** or for **non-compliance** (after giving a **reasonable chance to represent**).

**Declaration (s.10(5))**: **before any transaction** the authorised person must **ask for a declaration and information** that reasonably satisfy it the transaction is **not designed to contravene or evade** the Act. If the customer **refuses** or complies **unsatisfactorily**, it must **refuse in writing**, and **report to the Reserve Bank** if it thinks a contravention is planned.

**Misuse of purchased exchange (s.10(6))**: a customer who buys foreign exchange for a declared purpose and **does not use it for that purpose**, **does not surrender it in time**, or uses it for a **non-permissible** purpose is **deemed to have contravened** the Act.

**Directions (s.11)**: RBI can direct authorised persons and require information; **contravening a direction or failing to file a return** can cost up to **₹10,000** plus up to **₹2,000 a day** if continuing.

**Inspection (s.12)**: RBI may inspect an authorised person's business.

payload.title: Section 13: the penalty arithmetic
payload.core_explanation_md:
Anyone who **contravenes the Act, a rule, regulation, notification, direction or order, or a condition of an authorisation**, is liable **on adjudication** to:

- **up to three times the sum involved**, where the amount is **quantifiable**; or
- **up to ₹2 lakh**, where it is **not quantifiable**; and
- if the contravention **continues**, a **further penalty of up to ₹5,000 for every day after the first day**.

**Foreign assets above the prescribed threshold** (s.13(1A)): up to **three times the sum involved** and **confiscation of equivalent value in India**.

A way to remember: **3 times, ₹2 lakh, ₹5,000 a day after day one**.

payload.title: The dealing room: keeping dealers, books and records apart
payload.core_explanation_md:
RBI's Internal Control Guidelines rest on **one principle**: **separate the people who deal from the people who record, check and settle**.

- **Front office**: the **dealing room**.
- **Mid-office**: **risk management**, accounting policies and management information.
- **Back office**: **settlement, reconciliation and accounting**.

**Controls on dealers**
- **No accounting work** for dealers.
- **Deal slips** with broker, counterparty, currencies, amounts, **time**, rate and due dates, passed **without delay** to the back office.
- The **system stamps** the trading date, time and serial number; a dealer **cannot alter** them without authorisation. **Late deals** are marked and sent to an official **unconnected with the dealer**.
- **Voice recording**, tapes kept **at least two months** (longer if there is a dispute).
- An **annual break of two weeks or longer** for every dealer.
- Written acceptance of the **FEDAI and FIMMDA codes of conduct**.

payload.title: The back office and the brokers: confirmations, panels and brokerage
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Back office**
- **Independent confirmation** of contracts (except deals through **CCIL**); **dealers never sign confirmations**.
- Discrepancies **rectified the same day**; **no backlog**.
- **Rate-scan reports** at least **three times a day** where the system lacks the facility; deals at wide variance from market are questioned.

**Exchange brokers**
- **Cannot act as principals** or hold positions.
- **Broker's notes** received **before close of business** on the deal day and **reconciled the same day**.
- **No nominating** a broker for a deal not put through the broker.
- A panel of ideally **five or six** brokers, **reviewed annually**.
- **Dealing staff play no part** in scrutinising or paying **brokerage claims**; a **monthly broker-wise statement** goes to management.
- Brokers' malpractice goes to **FEDAI**.
- **Substituting** one bank for another in an inter-bank contract through a broker is **prohibited**.

payload.title: Risks in forex dealing and how limits and documents contain them
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Five risks**
1. **Credit**: **pre-settlement** (the **replacement cost** if the counterparty defaults before the deal settles) and **settlement** (paying **before** the counterparty does).
2. **Liquidity**: unable to fund or to **exit a position at a fair price**.
3. **Gap / interest rate**: moves in interest-rate differentials.
4. **Legal**: handled by **master agreements** (**ISDA, IFEMA, ICOM**).
5. **Operational**: systems and a **written contingency plan**.

**Limits**: set **globally** for local inter-bank and overseas business; **every dealer is told his limit**; deals are **counted against limits** and **aggregated at close of business**; **excesses are reported and approved**; **breaches of regulatory limits go to RBI**.

**Documents**: forwards up to **13 months** with customers need a **stamped contract note**; inter-bank, **unsigned computer confirmations plus a one-time stamped indemnity**. **Beyond 13 months** and for other derivatives, an **ISDA Master Agreement** with signed confirmations. Corporate clients give a **Board resolution** authorising their dealers.

payload.title: Nostro reconciliation, Vostro monitoring and audit
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Nostro reconciliation** (RBI calls it an **essential control**)
- **Statements at least weekly**, reconciled against the **mirror account** on the **same date**.
- Put routine items such as **export bills purchased** and **drafts issued** through **suspense accounts** to reduce unreconciled items.
- **No set-off** of debit and credit items and **no write-off** of unreconciled items to profit and loss except as RBI allows.
- A **monthly report** with **large** and **age-wise** unreconciled items.

**Vostro monitoring**: watch funds flow, **concealed overdrafts**, sudden changes in activity; assess correspondent banks' credit risk **at least once in twelve months**; get **balance confirmations**.

**Audit**: internal audit reviews limit excesses; a **special audit of the dealing room and its systems at least once a year**; **concurrent audit** is part of the **early warning system**.

payload.title: The two forex exposure limits and how the net open position is counted
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Net Overnight Open Position Limit (NOOPL)**: fixed by the **Board**, told to RBI, **not above 25% of total capital (Tier I and Tier II)**. It drives the **capital charge** on forex risk. A second limit for **rupee positions** (**NOP-INR**) may be prescribed by RBI.

**Counting the position**
1. For each currency add the **net spot**, **net forward** and **net options (delta-equivalent)** positions.
2. Convert each currency's and gold's net position into **rupees**.
3. Add all the **net short** positions, and separately all the **net long** positions.
4. The overall net position is the **higher** of the two sums (the **shorthand method**).
5. **Offshore** positions are worked out **separately** and **never netted** with onshore ones.

**Aggregate Gap Limit (AGL)**: set by the **Board**, **not above six times total capital**. Banks with **tenor-wise PV01 and VaR limits** may use those instead.

The **ALCO or an internal audit committee** monitors adherence.

payload.title: Working out a bank's net open position and its limits
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: at close of business a bank's net positions, converted into rupees, are: USD long ₹1,200 crore; EUR short ₹750 crore; JPY long ₹300 crore; GBP short ₹1,000 crore; gold long ₹150 crore. Its total capital (Tier I plus Tier II) is ₹6,400 crore. What is its overall net open position by the shorthand method, and what are the most the Board may fix for NOOPL and AGL?

worked_steps.description: Add the net long positions (USD, JPY, gold).
Add the net short positions (EUR, GBP).
The overall net position is the higher of the two sums.
Highest NOOPL the Board may fix: 25% of total capital.
Highest AGL: six times total capital.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The overall net open position is ₹1,750 crore (the higher of long ₹1,650 crore and short ₹1,750 crore); the Board may fix NOOPL at no more than ₹1,600 crore and AGL at no more than ₹38,400 crore. The position of ₹1,750 crore would exceed a NOOPL set at the maximum

self_check.prompt_text: What would the overall net position have been if the bank netted the longs against the shorts instead of taking the higher of the two sums?
self_check.expected_takeaway: ₹100 crore (1,750 − 1,650), which is wrong: the shorthand method takes the higher of the sums, not the difference.

payload.title: How large can a FEMA penalty be?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: (A) a person contravenes a direction in a transaction involving ₹4,50,000 and the amount is quantifiable. (B) Another contravention is not quantifiable and continues for 30 days. What is the maximum penalty in each case under section 13(1)?

worked_steps.description: A: up to three times the sum involved.
B: not quantifiable, so up to ₹2 lakh.
B: continuing for 30 days, the further penalty counts every day after the first, that is 29 days.
B: further penalty at ₹5,000 a day.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the count 29 days and not 30?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Act adds the daily penalty for every day after the first day.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is "foreign exchange" under the Act?

options.text_md: A bill of exchange drawn in Indian currency and payable in Indian currency in India
A bill of exchange drawn in Indian currency but payable in a foreign currency
A rupee cheque drawn on a resident's account
A rupee money order sent from one Indian city to another

payload.correct_explanation_md: Drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in a foreign currency are foreign exchange.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is NOT included in the Act's definition of "foreign exchange"?

options.text_md: A deposit payable in any foreign currency
options.explanation_md: Deposits, credits and balances payable in foreign currency are included.

options.text_md: A traveller's cheque drawn by a bank abroad but payable in Indian currency
A rupee balance held by a resident in a savings account in India
options.explanation_md: A rupee balance is Indian currency.

options.text_md: A letter of credit drawn in Indian currency but payable in a foreign currency

payload.correct_explanation_md: Rupee balances held in India are Indian currency; deposits payable in foreign currency and the listed instruments are foreign exchange.

payload.stem_md: A resident Indian transfers money abroad to buy a house there. How does the Act classify it?

options.text_md: A current account transaction, since money is simply paid abroad
options.explanation_md: Current account transactions do not alter assets or liabilities outside India.

options.text_md: Neither, since only the Reserve Bank can classify
A transaction outside the Act's scope
A capital account transaction, since it alters the resident's assets outside India
options.explanation_md: It creates an asset outside India.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A transaction that alters the assets or liabilities outside India of a person resident in India is a capital account transaction.

payload.stem_md: Under section 5, who may sell or draw foreign exchange to or from an authorised person for a current account transaction?

options.text_md: Any person, subject to reasonable restrictions the Central Government may impose in the public interest
Only persons resident in India
Only with RBI's prior approval in every case
options.explanation_md: Current account transactions are free, subject to restrictions.

options.text_md: Only authorised persons
options.explanation_md: The authorised person is the counterparty, not the only party.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Section 5 lets any person sell or draw foreign exchange for a current account transaction, with reasonable restrictions possible in the public interest.

payload.stem_md: A customer asks an authorised dealer for foreign exchange but refuses to give the declaration the dealer asked for. What must the dealer do under section 10(5)?

options.text_md: Proceed if the amount is small
Proceed and report afterwards
Refuse in writing, and report to the Reserve Bank if it believes a contravention is contemplated
Refuse orally and take no further action
options.explanation_md: The refusal must be in writing.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Where the person refuses or complies unsatisfactorily, the authorised person refuses in writing and reports to the Reserve Bank if it believes a contravention or evasion is contemplated.

payload.stem_md: Under section 13(1), what is the maximum penalty where the amount involved in a contravention is not quantifiable?

options.text_md: Up to three times the sum involved
Up to Rs two lakh, with a further Rs 5,000 for each day after the first day if it continues
Up to Rs 10,000 plus Rs 2,000 a day
options.explanation_md: That is the penalty under section 11 on authorised persons.

options.text_md: Up to Rs 50,000

payload.correct_explanation_md: Where the amount is not quantifiable the penalty is up to Rs two lakh, plus up to Rs 5,000 for every day after the first day of a continuing contravention.

payload.stem_md: What is the cardinal principle of RBI's Internal Control Guidelines for forex dealing?

options.text_md: Dealers must do their own accounting for speed
options.explanation_md: Dealers should not do accounting work.

options.text_md: One officer should deal and confirm for efficiency
Rotation of dealers every month
options.explanation_md: Rotation is a separate control; the cardinal principle is segregation.

options.text_md: Clear functional segregation of dealing, mid-office, back-office, accounting and reconciliation

payload.correct_explanation_md: The cardinal principle is clear functional segregation of dealing, mid-office, back-office (processing and control), accounting and reconciliation.

payload.stem_md: For how long should recordings of dealing room conversations be preserved, at the least?

options.text_md: One week
Six months in all cases
At least two months, and until the issue is resolved where a dispute has been raised
One year in all cases

payload.correct_explanation_md: Tapes may be preserved for at least two months and, where a dispute has been raised, until it is resolved.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about exchange brokers is consistent with the Guidelines?

options.text_md: Brokers may take positions to provide liquidity
options.explanation_md: They are prohibited from doing so.

options.text_md: Brokers may not act as principals or maintain positions in foreign currencies
Dealers may scrutinise and pay brokerage claims themselves
options.explanation_md: Dealing staff should have nothing to do with it.

options.text_md: A broker may substitute one bank for another in an inter-bank contract

payload.correct_explanation_md: Exchange brokers are prohibited from acting as principals and maintaining positions; substitution of banks in inter-bank contracts is prohibited.

payload.stem_md: A bank performs its side of a foreign exchange contract before the counterparty has done so, and the counterparty fails to deliver. Which risk has materialised?

options.text_md: Settlement risk
options.explanation_md: Settlement risk arises when a bank performs before the counterparty.

options.text_md: Pre-settlement risk
options.explanation_md: Pre-settlement risk is the replacement cost if the counterparty defaults during the life of the contract.

options.text_md: Liquidity risk
options.explanation_md: Liquidity risk is not being able to fund or exit at a reasonable price.

options.text_md: Legal risk
options.explanation_md: Legal risk concerns enforceability and documentation.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Settlement risk is the risk of loss arising when a bank performs on its obligation under a contract before the counterparty does.

payload.stem_md: A bank enters into a forward contract of 18 months with a corporate customer. What documentation do RBI's guidelines call for between a bank and such a customer?

options.text_md: A stamped contract note only
options.explanation_md: That is for forward contracts of up to 13 months.

options.text_md: Unsigned computer confirmations with a one-time stamped indemnity
options.explanation_md: That is for inter-bank deals up to 13 months.

options.text_md: No documentation
An ISDA Master Agreement with signed confirmations for each transaction
options.explanation_md: Tenors above 13 months need an ISDA Master Agreement.

payload.correct_explanation_md: For forward contracts exceeding 13 months with customers other than retail or individual customers, banks should enter into an ISDA Master Agreement and obtain signed confirmations.

payload.stem_md: How often should a bank at least receive statements from correspondent banks for Nostro reconciliation, and against what are they reconciled?

options.text_md: Monthly, against the general ledger
options.explanation_md: Statements are received at least weekly and reconciled to the mirror account.

options.text_md: Daily, against the vostro statement
options.explanation_md: Not the stated frequency or record.

options.text_md: At least weekly, against the mirror account on the same date
Annually, against the audit report

payload.correct_explanation_md: Bank statements should be received at least weekly and reconciled with the mirror account choosing the same date for both.

payload.stem_md: What is the highest net overnight open position limit (NOOPL) an authorised dealer's Board may fix?

options.text_md: Six times total capital
options.explanation_md: That is the ceiling for the aggregate gap limit.

options.text_md: 25 per cent of total capital (Tier I and Tier II)
50 per cent of total capital
Ten per cent of net worth

payload.correct_explanation_md: The NOOPL fixed by the Board must not exceed 25 per cent of the total capital of the authorised dealer.

payload.stem_md: By the shorthand method, how is the overall net foreign exchange position found?

options.text_md: Subtract total shorts from total longs
options.explanation_md: The method takes the higher sum, not the difference.

options.text_md: Take the largest single currency position
Add all positions ignoring sign
Add all net short positions and all net long positions separately, and take the higher of the two sums

payload.correct_explanation_md: The overall net foreign exchange position is the higher of the sum of all net short positions and the sum of all net long positions.

payload.stem_md: An authorised dealer has total capital (Tier I and Tier II) of ₹9,200 crore. What is the highest aggregate gap limit (AGL) its Board may fix, in rupees crore?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: AGL must not exceed six times total capital: 9,200 × 6 = 55,200.

payload.stem_md: A bank's net positions in rupees crore are: long 840, long 215, short 560, short 700. By the shorthand method, what is its overall net open position, in rupees crore?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Sum of longs 840 + 215 = 1,055; sum of shorts 560 + 700 = 1,260; the overall position is the higher: 1,260.

payload.stem_md: A contravention is not quantifiable and continues for 45 days. What is the maximum penalty under section 13(1), in rupees?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Up to ₹2,00,000, plus ₹5,000 for every day after the first: 44 × 5,000 = ₹2,20,000. Total ₹4,20,000.

unresolved: The RBI Internal Control Guidelines of 3 February 2011 are the only published text of the dealing room controls found; RBI's page still hosts them (updated 13 November 2026) but its 2025 consolidation could not be searched for a withdrawal notice, and some of its content (for example references to the 1996 revision, Rate-Scan reports and FEDAI dealing hours) predates later changes; items state the Guidelines and do not test the dated details.

The NOOPL (25 per cent of total capital) and AGL (six times total capital) come from the Master Direction page updated on 1 October 2026; earlier versions of the page were not retrieved, so a change after the 30 June 2026 cut-off cannot be excluded. The courseware (printed pp. 14-16) was read in earlier batches and describes the same limits in general terms.
The compounding limit stated in the courseware (printed p. 48) is from RBI's compounding guidelines of April 2025 and is not in the Act; it is not taught.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
